Hon. CHARLES STEW7ART (Minister of the Interior) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 199, to amend the Dominion Lands
Act.
Explain.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The purpose of this amendment is to permit the extension of the homesteading privilege to others than those mentioned in the amendment of 1925. It is to extend the privilege of granting a second homestead to those who have proven up prior to January 1, 1928. This is being done in order to meet the request of a large number of people in the prairie provinces who think that this privilege should be extended to allow farmers and their families to move into the northern portions of the district, and the father of the family to secure a second homestead.
The other amendment is a minor one with respect to school lands.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.
Mr. T. L. CHURCH (Toronto Northwest) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 200 to amend the Insurance Act (lapsed policies).
Explain.

The object of this amendment is to require annually a sworn statement by insurance companies of their lapsed policies. Of the new business written annually, forty to fifty per cent is lapsed, surrendered or confiscated. This bill gives the superintendent of insurance power not only to check up the revenues, but also to protect the policy holders who have paid in less than three years' premiums, and who at present lose all the premiums they have paid in if they should happen to be out of work and are unable to continue paying the premiums. This will be a protection both to the public and the government.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

I desire, Mr. Speaker, to speak
to a question of privilege. I have been interested in public affairs in this country for some thirty-three years, and during that time I have always been ready, when my opponents met me on the political platform or elsewhere, to extend to them the courtesies which I expected from them. Yesterday afternoon, when the resolution of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Euler) was under discussion, dealing with proposed amendments to the Customs Act, the hon. member for West Hamilton (Mr. Bell) in my absence arose in his place and made certain statements. Those statements wfill be found at page 1892 of Hansard of yesterday. First, the hon. member said:
Then will the minister inform the committee if there was no breach of the Canadian law when the steamer Kennedy was taken in for hovering in the Northumberland straits with $20,000 worth of Scotch whiskey belonging to a company of which the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough was president?
A little further on will be found the second statement:
If the minister is correct in that, perhaps he will be able to inform the committee why the $20,000 worth of wet goods carried by the Kennedy was afterwards handed back?
Now, Mr. Speaker, as I said a moment ago,
I was not in the house yesterday to answer those statements. If they are true, I would have nothing more to say; if they are untrue, then the language permissible to me under the

Privilege-Mr. Duff
rules is not sufficiently strong to express my indignation. Of course, I regret that the hon. member is not in his place, and I would gladly wait for him to take his seat if I were not afraid that my hon. friend the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Euler) will not within the next fortnight or month be in a position to go on with the legislation amending the Customs Act which is now before the house. Consequently I feel that in fairness to myself I must deal with this matter immediately.
Two years ago, during the course of the general election, the hon. gentleman addressed a public meeting in my home town of Lunenburg, where he had full opportunity to deal with the Kennedy matter, but seated with him on the platform were prominent Conservatives of the locality, and throughout his speech he never once dealt with smuggling, boot-legging and rum-running on the Atlantic or Pacific coast; he confined himself entirely to what had been taking place on the Quebec border. That shows the courage of the hon. gentleman. Yesterday he said:
-the steamer Kennedy was taken in for hovering in the Northumberland straits-*
I deny absolutely that the steamer Kennedy was taken into Pictou for hovering in the Northumberland straits during any period. There is no such vessel as the steamer Kennedy.
The W. C. Kennedy.

Don't worry; I am coming to it; take your medicine. There was a schooner called the W. C. Kennedy-and this is not the first time that a few of my Tory friends have referred to it. It was brought up before the special committee of this house which investigated the customs department in the session of 1936. It was also brought up by some more of my Conservative friends before the customs commission, and last year I had the privilege of coming to Ottawa, at the country's expense, and giving evidence before the commission with regard to the W. C. Kennedy.
It is quite true 'that I had the schooner W. C. Kennedy built in the year 1920 for parties in Newfoundland, but as they could not take delivery of her I formed a company to take over the boat. She is a little three-masted schooner. If I remember correctly, I sold the W. C. Kennedy in 1923, about six months before she was illegally seized- mark you, not legally, but illegally seized- in Northumberland straits, nine and a half miles east by south of Pictou island. At the time of this illegal seizure I had no interest whatever in the schooner, and I had nothing rMr. Duff.]
whatever to do with paying the deposit of $400, which I have been accused of doing, not openly by a few individuals but surreptitiously.	,
Now, sir, the really serious charge is that I was president of a company which owned $20,000 worth of scotch whiskey, or, to put it in the words of the bon. member for West Hamilton:
-$20,000 worth of Scotch whiskey belonging to a company of which the hon. member for Antigonish-G-uysborough was president.
I say that this statement is not true. Perhaps under the rules I cannot characterize it as false, but I do say that it is absolutely untrue; there is not a scintilla of truth in it.
I never was an officer of any company or any body of individuals that purchased Scotch whiskey or liquor of any kind to smuggle into Canada. I was never the president of, nor had I any connection with, any company that smuggled liquor into Canada. I never had any connection with any person who either purchased, smuggled or sold or handled whiskey or any other liquor in Canada. Before the commission in Ottawa I made a sworn statement that I never bought liquors, that I never smuggled liquors to sell, and that I never sold liquors. Under the circumstances I submit, Mr. Speaker, that it is grossly unfair for any hon. gentleman to get up on the floor and make such unfounded statements in respect to another member which cannot be proven, as was done by the hon. member for West Hamilton, in respect to myself.

Mr. T. L. CHURCH (Toronto Northwest) moved;
That, in the opinion of this house, immediate action should he taken, without further and unnecessary delays, to enter into a treaty with the government of the United States for the immediate development and generation of water-power on the St. Lawrence river and its deepening and development in the interests of navigation, and that a greater St. Lawrence *waterway is an immediate and economic necessity for the welfare and best interests of Canada.
And that this house is further of the opinion that the government should undertake the construction and operation of this canal as a

St. Lawrence Waterway-Mr. Church
public undertaking itself and the power incident herein should be developed and generated at cost by the government for the people under public ownership and not alienated to private interests for gain or exported for use outside Canada.
He said: This resolution, Mr. Speaker, deals with one of the most important questions to come before the people of Canada since confederation, and I am sorry that more time cannot be found in which to discuss it. This is admitted to be the greatest economic problem facing the people of the North American continent to-day. It should not be considered as a political or party matter; it is not a local or provincial question but a great economic matter which affects every man, woman and child in the two great countries bordering on the great lakes. We have time to discuss all kinds of academia subjects which are brought up during the session, but we find very little time to devote to basic problems such as this, which will affect many of the great activities of our country. We have a great many rules and regulations in this house, some of them over one hundred years old1; no one can bring up any question for the good of the country without being reminded that someone made a rule or regulation many years ago which has the effect of preventing a discussion of that particular matter. This question, however, is all-important, and should be approached from the national standpoint of the greatest good to the greatest number. We are not allowed to bring up any question in which the matter of finance is involved, but as we all know almost everything we would like to bring up has to do with the finances of the country in one way or the other. Just a few moments ago we found that the question of finance has something to do with even our own little restaurant question. Nothing can be taken up in this house without bringing up the question of money; under our rules only the government can bring up such matters. When a private member tries to do something to help solve some of the great economic problems of the country the Prime Minister will get up and throw a few bouquets, after which he will tell us that the question affects the finances of the country and therefore cannot be discussed. Handicapped and hemmed in as we are in this house by our antiquated rules and regulations, which are contained in the dead text books of the past, it is very hard for a member of parliament to discharge his duty to his constituents in considering any of these great problems which lie before us.
Never in the history of the party system in this country has such a great opportunity
come to any political party to solve one of the great, outstanding problems of our nation.
I would that Canada had an Adam Beck at present to take up this question which deals with power, light and transportation; I would that Canada had a Mussolini, who would do something in a practical way for the people of this country. Instead, we have a government which relies on the law courts for the solution of problems of this kind. The question of the Alberta natural resources is on its way to the Privy Council and no one knows when it will come back again; in the meantime we are not allowed to discuss it. Is this a free parliament or is it not? Are we attending a mock parliament or a real parliament? If we are free, any member should be able to speak on questions of this kind without waiting for some court to bring in a decision.
We also have boards of strategy on some sides of this house, and we are not supposed to bring up anvthing which has not been approved by these boards. We had one such board on this side of the house, which used to bring up questions which kept us here until three or four o'clock in the morning, and no one was allowed to think for himself. Even then, most of the problems which were brought up were not heard of outside the walls of this building. What was the result? When the ballots were counted we found ourselves over here in this Potter s field.
Matters have not improved since we obtained our new status; we now have a minister plenipotentiary in Washington, from whom we can hardly secure the production of papers or any information as to what is going on. There has been a great change m the form of the returns made by our new representatives as compared with those which we formerly received from the British Ambassador in Washington. Our representative signs himself "Envoy Extraordinary." He is extraordinary, in my opinion. He is also our minister plenipotentiary, but wha,t has he been doing in connection with this matter? We have spent millions of dollars on officials, commissions, mock parliaments and so on, yet we have had only one report dealing with this matter. To my fellow members on this side of the house I would say that unless we are up and doing the Liberal party will carry through this great undertaking. We will have an election in a few years, and I believe that within a few weeks we will have at least a declaration from hon. gentlemen opposite that an agreement has been negotiated dealing with this all-important matter.
Why should these matters be referred to the Privy Council? That tribunal seems to
1928	COMMONS
St. Lawrence Waterway-Mr. Church
be a very handy agency to take up these matters and throw out a life-line to the government of the day when they do not wish parliament to discuss them. In my opinion the political party which takes up this question in earnest will foe in power in this country for a good many years, and I think we should be devoting all our energies to that end. The development of the St. Lawrence outranks in importance all other questions in the public life of this Dominion,, past or present. Now is the time to deal with it, because it is vitally important that it be settled at the earliest possible moment. I hope this question will be brought up again, and I also hope that before it comes up in the house next time the government will see fit to have representatives of the Senate and the House of Commons go to Brockville or Prescott, where they can board a steamer and proceed directly to the places where these operations will take place, because seeing is believing.
Mr. Hoover visited the scene and he is a gentleman who now stands as one of the heads of the great Republican party, had an open mind on this problem, but after going through the ship canal with us and seeing the plans and the work being done on the Welland canal, he became, as he is to-day, a warm supporter of this waterway from the business and the economic standpoints.
There are certain questions which should be answered. What is the seaway? Is such a deep channel necessary? What must be done to improve it? What will it cost? How is an international agreement made? What agreement is necessary? Can we afford the seaway? And then it will be proper to say a few words on the political side of this question, on the engineering features, on the economic and international phases and to discuss briefly how it reacts upon the labour market.
A few years ago-on the 26th of April, 1922 -there was a debate in this house on a similar resolution of mine. The arguments in favour of this waterway were set out by me then along the lines I mentioned a moment ago.
Since then we have had strong reports made in favour of this improvement by the International Joint Commission representatives of both countries, which prove conclusively from an engineering standpoint, from the power standpoint, and from an economic standpoint that this particular highway to the sea is necessary and practical. The great advantage of the St. Lawrence river is that it is one of the principal natural waterways to the sea. The cost should be divided between the two

countries. It is a speed highway, avoiding long delays. We have engineering and commercial assurance of three facts: first, that it can be done, that it is practicable; second, that the cost will be less than that for any other route which has been spoken of; and third, that it will make possible the development of millions of horsepower and the saving of millions of tons of coal every year.
Canada has dealt differently with railway traffic from what it has with water-borne traffic. In the case of water-borne traffic, our canal system does not reveal any well developed policy. The deepening of the Welland canal is an important link in the St. Lawrence scheme and should have been finished long ago if the work had been prosecuted with the same vigour which marked the development of the Chippewa-Queenston power canal. There have been some objections raised to it. Some say it will be an economic failure and a waste of public money. The answer to that is that the power alone will pay for the work, and that is set out in the report of the International Joint Commission. Then it is said that the cost of power will be prohibitive, The answer to that is that the commission's report says it will not be.
Then it is charged that the fogs and ice make the St. Lawrence route too hazardous to be of practical use; although it is admitted that it is all right for six or seven months. The answer is that the fogs and ice on the Atlantic play havoc with the steamship service there as well.
It is objected that ocean vessels cannot navigate the restricted channels or afford the delays of lockage in canals. The reply is that the objection is not sound, the report says so, and it deals to the extent of twenty pages with that argument.
It is said that there will be no return tonnage and that one-way traffic cannot be developed. The answer is that the west is a great consumer and there will be a new development of package freight, and a new type of ship which will be able to sail the lakes and the ocean as well. We have a great many old whaleback type boats now sailing the great lakes and going down to the Atlantic seaboard.
The statement is made that the purpose is to enable Canada to control the export grain trade. The answer is that that is not so.
It is asserted that the project is designed to destroy the competition of the barge canal. The answer is that it would cater to a different form of trade and would be a feeder to the barge canal.

St. Lawrence Waterway-Mr. Church
Then it is said that the power is not needed. The answer is given by the Ontario HydroElectric Power Commission.
The last objection is that it would expose the United States to the peril of invasion by Great Britain. The answer is that we have had a hundred years of peace between the United States and Canada, and we have been digging canals for over a hundred years. There is only one difference between this canal and the others, and that is that it is proposed to be a little deeper.
I might say that I cannot understand some of the objections to entering into the particular treaty which is urged here; they are more parochial than anything else. For the past hundred years and more the two nations have jointly been using the St. Lawrence river and the improvements therein made. Treaties have been entered into, all matters of navigation and rights have been negotiated. To-day it is not a question, as I view it, of getting or giving an advantage, but it is a matter of continuing the policy that is as old as the two nations, that of using the waters of the St. Lawrence jointly and freely for the benefit of both nations. Neither government will forfeit a single right or privilege which they now have, in order that the two governments may jointly develop this river. Whether a ditch is to be four or thirty feet deep does not involve any new international or political question; or whether the improvement is on the American side or the Canadian side, or which government spends the money.
You are not breaking any new ground in entering into this new agreement. You are not raising any new international questions. I could quote from international treaties from 1792 till the present time to substantiate that point. We are not charting a new course, we are not raising new international questions, but we are travelling a road which has been used for a hundred years. All we are asking you to do is to modernize and bring up to date these channels so that the public and commerce can use them.
The last joint reports of the engineers representing the two governments, in 1921 and 1924 and 1926, both support locating a major part of the improvements on what may be called the international section on the United States side of the international boundary. Whether the international section will be on the Canadian side or on the American side, does not matter very much. On the Canadian side there must be a straight right of way; but on the American side it will be a curved course. Whether the one or the other is adopted is a matter for further negotiation between the governments; and I do not know
what the new report says about that. It is interesting to note, however, that according to the engineers, for economic reasons, it should be on the American side. I want it in Canada if possible. I do not believe that the United States or Canada wishes to take any advantage on that account. All that it desired is to take advantage of this opportunity to benefit navigation. The first move is to negotiate a treaty. That is set out in the first clause of the resolution.
If there was less red tape between 'Washington and Ottawa we would have had all the papers on the table long ago. Are we to wait until they appear in the United States newspapers, or are we to get them on the table of the house now? The engineers who made this international report of 1922 rejected the New York plan and adopted the St. Lawrence plan. The case for the St. Lawrence plan has been set forth; it has weathered every possible opposition and attack on both sides of the border, and it stands to-day approved. We have to-day economic emancipation written across the face of this report. It has taken seven years of hard and insistent fighting, but the case of the St. Lawrence has been made and won. The fight has been worth the struggle for it has meant striking the shackles from forty million people in this land. The last and most pleasant task is that of bringing the two nations together in treaty. Let us write a new chapter in world peace, in international co-operation, in econo-' mics. Let us unlock a new treasure house of wealth. If the party on this side of the house will not undertake this work, the government has the greatest opportunity that any party ever had in its history.
A few minutes ago I asked the question: What is this seaway? From the head of the lakes at Port Arthur and Fort William across the ocean as far as Liverpool it covers a distance of 4,500 miles, and there is deep water navigation over all that distance with the exception of two short sections. One is at the old Welland canal, where the canal is fourteen feet deep, and the other is a twenty-four mile strip between Prescott and Cornwall. On the Welland canal section this country is spending $133,000,000 for a new canal. Our contention is that these two shallow sections of the waterway exclude us from the ocean, and because of the limited size of the eastern section it becomes necessary for cargoes from the upper lakes to be transhipped at Port Colborne. This double transfer is slow and expensive; it means extra delay and labour, and at best only a portion of the great lakes commerce finds its way through Port Colborne to the sea. Af
1930	COMMONS
St. Lawrence Waterway-Mr. Church
a result of this we are losing business to our competitors, the United States, at Buffalo through the Erie canal.
A deep channel is necessary. A start has been made on the Welland canal, and the first half of the greater St. Lawrence waterway, namely, the Welland canal, is well on the way to completion. The second half of the shallow waterway is the twenty-four mile stretch between Prescott and Cornwall. The St. Lawrence seaway is to take the place of the fourteen-foot St. Lawrence canal now in use and to continue the deep channel of the upper lakes on to the Atlantic. Its completion will permit great lakes' ships to reach ocean ports on the lower St. Lawrence, and will allow ocean-going ships of less than 27-foot draught to enter the great lakes. The physical effect will be to make the ports of the great lakes ocean ports. It will give to them, and to the fanners and manufacturers in the interior, the benefit of ocean rates to overseas markets. The economic effect will be to lower transportation costs. The seaway will increase the returns to the producer. It will foster new enterprise; it will throw open new markets; it will permit a normal development of our national life, and in general it will promote the common welfare.
What has to be done is to develop the two short strips at Welland and at Prescott, and also at the Galops islands and rapids which I have mentioned to-day. It is agreed that this is the best solution of the problem. I do not wish to dilate now on the rival plans. It is considered advisable to start this St. Lawrence plan with the twenty-four mile stretch from Prescott to Cornwall and the power development from the work will pay its share of the construction cost of the improvement. The report says that the scheme will cost 1264,000,000. If you deduct the value of the inherent power which will be developed, the cost for a good seaway will be $123,000,000. The cost of this improvement, if built as a twenty-seven foot ship channel alone, and without any power, would be $173,000,000. By developing power in the international section and charging its fair share of the combined cost of navigation and' power to power, and building the rest of the seaway without power, the navigation cost is reduced to $123,000,000. If power is developed in the Canadian section, this entire navigation cost will be increased and the canal distance shortened, thus providing better navigation at an effective net cost chargeable to navigation amounting to $148,000,000. Thus you have a cost of $123,000,000 for a good seaway, or $148,000,000 for a better seaway.

Before this work is gone ahead with, an agreement must be made between the United States and Canada. I asked a few moments ago:	How is an international agreement to
be reached? Under the constitution of the United States, the president has full power to negotiate a treaty with Canada, stating the terms and conditions under which the seaway is to be constructed. The agreement then goes to the senate, where, in order to be ratified, it must receive a two-thirds vote of those present. The Canadian procedure is for the government of the day, speaking for the party in power, to enter into the treaty desired, and to submit the agreement to both houses of parliament for majority vote approval. What agreement is necessary? By treaties already existing, particularly the Washington treaty of 1871 and the Boundary treaty of 1909, the two nations have defined their rights, duties and privileges with respect to the great lakes-St. Lawrence waterway, including the canals and locks, uniting them into one highway of commerce. In either case the only requirement is that the civil laws of either country shall be observed by the citizens of the other while making use of waters that for navigation purposes are declared by these treaties to be equally and jointly the property of both.
The only question outstanding between the two nations is that of further improvement of a waterway already improved, but inadequate for the traffic now demanding passage [DOT] and originating within the interior of both nations. It is merely a question of detail what plan of improvement shall be adopted, where the money shall be spent, and how the construction work shall be administered. It differs from preceding improvements in this, that in all other cases, that is the locks at Sault Ste Marie or the new Welland canal, either government could and did complete the job single-handed. The United States government did the work in the case of the locks at Sault Ste Marie and the Canadian government in the case of the locks in the Niagara district. In the case of the St Lawrence seaway, the international boundary, the course of the river channel, the problems of dam construction, all combine to make joint improvement both necessary and desirable.
Details of agreement as to plans, details respecting the joint outlay and supervision of the joint improvement while building, furnish the reasons for a further agreement between the two people. No additional rights or privileges are necessary to either nation; no concession of any territorial or jurisdictional rights is called for on the part of

St. Lawrence Waterway-Mr. Church
either nation. All that is required is a written agreement as to when and by what means the seaway already existing and in use shall be enlarged and made equal to the requirements of modern commerce.
Can we afford the seaway? Yes. The power inherent will pay for the construction. Is it practicable? The St. Lawrence commission of the United States in its report to the president under date of December 27, 1926, state:
The construction of a shipway of sufficient depth to admit ocean shipping from the Atlantic to the great lakes will lessen the economic handicaps of adverse transportation costs of a vast area in the interior of the continent. Within the United States it embraces all or large portions of the states of Ohio, Indiana, Kentucky, Illinois, Iowa, Missouri, Kansas, Nebraska, North and South Dakota, Montana, Wisconsin, Minnesota, Michigan, Pennsylvania and New York. It includes a large part of Canada. Within this area there are more than forty million inhabitants who gain their livelihood from its basic industries. It produces a vast surplus both from agriculture and from manufactures, much of which demands long transportation. It has been estimated that the values in a single year to the farmers alone would equal the capital cost of the waterway.
The conclusion of the commission is as follows:
The construction of the shipway from the .great lakes to the sea is imperative both for the relief and for the future development of a vast area in the interior of the continent.
hat will Canada do? We do not know. The best answer to this question is to state just what Canada has already done. Canada has been digging for a hundred years and all Canada would have to do would be to join in more digging for a deeper canal between the two countries. The Great Lakes-St. Lawrence route has been used as a highway of commerce since first discovered.
In 1779 Canada began building canals and locks to pass the rapids in the upper St. Lawrence. Before the end of the eighteenth century she built the first lock at the Soo. Between that time and the present she has built and twice enlarged the Welland, built and twice enlarged the St. Lawrence canals, built the modern Canadian lock at the Soo, improved the lower St. Lawrence from the ocean to Montreal, and has only recently let the contracts for the last portion of the 27-foot Welland ship canal now building. This has cost Canada not less than $230,000,000, of which amount $115,600,000 is chargeable to the unfinished Welland ship canal, due for completion in 1930. In the meantime the United States has expended at the Soo and in the main channels of the great lakes, $44,-
700,000.
Now I come to the international treaties of which I spoke. Time will not permit me to read them all, but I will mention them. Let me first ask, what has so far been done toward making the great lakes and the St. Lawrence an international highway for commerce? If we look at these treaties respecting the great lakes, the connecting rivers and the St. Lawrence river, it will be found that the free and mutual use of the great lakes and of the St. Lawrence river has been enjoyed by the people of Canada and of the United States from the time of the close of the revolution until the present day. It is true that disputes have arisen. It is true that laws passed by the one country or the other have been looked upon as restrictive, but the fact remains that never in all that time has the actual use of the St. Lawrence or of the great lakes and their connecting channels been denied by either nation to the citizens of the other. That fact is of profound significance, for while the " natural " right to navigate the lower St. Lawrence was denied to the citizens of the United States by Great Britain, the privilege and the practical use of that channel was not denied.
The legal title of the United States in the great lakes and in the St. Lawrence rests upon a firm foundation. That great highway was once completely within the possession of France, secured to her by right of discovery. In 1763 all right and title to the dominions of France east of the Mississippi passed to Great Britain. Twenty years later, by the treaty of 1782, the British dominions in North America were divided and the boundary line between the new nation of the United States and the remaining British possessions was indicated as the mid-channel of the great lakes and the connecting waters, including the St. Lawrence to the northern boundary of New York.
By clause 8 of the treaty of 1782 it was agreed that:
The navigation of the river Mississippi, from its source to the ocean, shall forever remain free and open to the subjects of Great Britain and the citizens of the United States.
Then we have the treaty of 1794, known as the Jay treaty, which provided for joint relations. Then in 1814 the treaty of Ghent sets out the rights of the parties with respect to the St. Lawrence, and by article 2 provides:
The intercourse between the United States and his Britannic Majesty's possessions in the West Indies and on the continent of North America shall not be affected, but each party shall remain in the complete possession of its rights with respect to such an intercourse.
In 1817 the Rush-Bagot agreement for limitation of naval armaments on the great lakes

1932	COMMONS
St. Lawrence Waterway-Mr. Church
was proclaimed, and since that time these international waters have been without gun or ship or fortress intended as a threat on the part of either toward the other.
In the treaty of 1842 the mind of the two nations is still further shown as drawing together to one common purpose, when in article 2 of that treaty they agree:
It being understood that all the water communications and all the usual portages along the line from lake Superior to the lake of the Woods, and also Grand Portage, from the shore of lake Superior to the Pigeon river, as now actually used, shall be free and open to the use of the citizens and subjects of both countries.
Again, by article 3 of that same treaty, the river St. John forming part of the boundary between the United States and Canada, and in part a stream wholly within the province of New Brunswick, was declared "free and open to both parties and shall in no way be obstructed by either." Article 7 of the same treaty declares that the channels in the river St. Lawrence on both sides of the Long Sault islands and of Barnhart island, as well as the channels in the river Detroit on both sides of the island Bois Blanc, and between that island and both the American and Canadian shores, and the channels between the various islands lying near the junction of the river St. Clair with the lake of that name, shall be free and open to the ships and the vessels of both parties.
Then we have what is known as the Reciprocity treaty, which reaffirmed the same rights. Then in 1871, the Washington treaty was concluded, and article 27 of that treaty provides that the commerce of both nations shall enjoy common and equal rights and privileges within the canals or navigable waters of either. Here we have in this treaty of 1871 the bedrock of common property rights to the navigation of the St. Lawrence as distinguished from any possession or claim of possession of rights extending beyond navigation, upon which to establish the lasting structure of an agreement that will provide a seaway from the great lakes to the Atlantic.
The duty of both nations is to improve the St. Lawrence. But the story is not yet complete. Once more the two nations met in 1909 and concluded the boundary waterways treaty, which reaffirmed the doctrine that the United States and Great Britain have joint rights both as to navigation and power in these rivers. I would direct the attention of the house to the last paragraph of that treaty, which reads as follows:
It is further agreed that so long as this treaty shall remain in force, this same right of navigation shall extend to the waters of lake

Michigan and to all canals connecting boundary waters now existing or which may hereafter be constructed on either side of the line.
It will be noted that the language of the treaty covers canals "which may hereafter be constructed." We possess now every navigation right necessary. Police power we do not seek. The Welland canal, for instance, is wholly within Canada, and the police powers are under the jurisdiction of Canada. We have used these canals for nearly one hundred years and there has never been any trouble. This United States bogey has been raised by a lot of the power interests and the electric ring, and they have done more to bring this electric ring into Canada than any other agency.
What is the United States prepared to do? The United States has expended, in the dredged channels of the Great Lakes between lake Superior and lake Erie, $44,000,000. We have spent $230,000,000 on our canals.
I notice that an important declaration was made in favour of the St. Lawrence waterway by the chairman of the Montreal harbour board, Hon. W. L. McDougald. The arguments that have been used against the development of this waterway have been largely parochial. The Hon. Mr. McDougald takes very strong ground in favour of this waterway. He quotes the report of the joint commission, as follows:
As to the economic practicability of the waterways, the commission finds that, without considering the probability of new traffic created by the opening of a water route to the seaboard, there exists to-day between the region economically tributary to the great lakes and overseas points, as well as between the same region and the Atlantic and the Pacific seaboard, a volume of outbound and inbound trade that might reasonably be expected to seek this route sufficient to justify the expense involved in its improvement.

I give it as my considered opinion as chairman of the board of harbour commissioners of Montreal, and as the opinion of the technical staff of the harbour commission, who are in daily touch with shipping and of the moving of various commodities in and out of that port, that the business of that port will not be diminished, but on the contrary will steadily increase from year to year, and the proposed deepening of the St. Lawrence waterways will greatly accelerate the rate of increase jn the volume of business handled by Canadas national port of Montreal. One of the main factors in achieving this beneficial result will be the undoubted lowering of the costs of the all-water grain movement from the head of the lakes, the minimum estimate of which, arrived at by all authorities, is a saving of three cents a bushel. Many experts say the saving will be as high as six cents a bushel but we are sure it will be at least three.
That is also the figure which the joint commission estimated.
Why is the lake Erie basin much more highly industrialized than the Ontario basin? Simply because it has the benefit of these deep waterways, with the result that Toledo, Detroit, Buffalo and other cities in that basin are large industrial centres.

Mr. Speaker, should we consider the wording of the resolution of the hon. member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church), we are naturally led to believe that he wants the United States to put up half the necessary expenditure to build a dam across the Long Sault rapids and dredge a canal 27 feet deep, from Montreal to the head of the Great Lakes. Secondly ....

Secondly, after the project is completed, he wants this enterprise to be owned by the state, and that Canada alone should reap the benefits. He seems to forget the aspirations of our neighbours and ignore one of their mottoes.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to a
point of order. I started to speak at a quarter to four, and it is now only twenty past four. I looked at my watch and at the clock when I rose.

I have the officers of the House to guide me in this matter. The hon. gentleman spoke for forty-one minutes.

He
seems to forget their aspirations and ignore one of their mottoes which is part of their institution: "If you want a thing well done, do it yourself."
Judging from the tenor of his resolution, we might have expected that he would give proof of the urgency of his project and that he was also prepared to silence, in forty minutes, objections of a constitutional or physical nature but especially those of an international order. He did not do so. First, in regard to the constitutional viewpoint, the attitude he takes in this house seems to me untimely, owing to the fact that the provinces inter-tested in this project, according to the jurisprudence recently enacted in connection with the ownership of shores and beds of navigable rivers, forces the Dominion government not to interfere as long as the general interest of the country is not at stake.
Now, none of the provinces which are free to act in this matter have, at present, taken any official stand in regard to this project. Until the Privy Council has made up its mind we can but look upon this resolution as being out of order.
Moreover, considering that this resolution implies an expenditure of public money, I doubt, according to the rules of the house, that a private member has a right to submit such a measure.
From the physical standpoint, we cannot assert that the construction of a dam across the Long Sault rapids is beyond the reach of civil engineering. However, we may venture to say that at this spot nature would create such serious difficulties in the way of such an enterprise as to render it both uncertain and detrimental to the country's interest.
On December 15, 1908, Messrs. Anderson, Lafleur and Butler, engineers of the Department of Marine, made a report to the Dominion government wdiich in substance was, that no one could forsee the consequences of the building of a dam with artificial causeways in the narrowest parts of the St. Lawrence, at Long Sault, where an immense sheet of water remains opened during the severe cold of our winters.
In fact, in that portion of international territory which extends between Prescott and Goose Neck Island, we have in winter, 18 miles of open water and a stretch of 13 miles of ice; between Goose Neck Island and Cornwall, we have 6 miles of open water and 15 miles of ice. In the open water frazil and

St. Lawrence Waterway-Mr. Deslauriers
anchor-ice form during the whole winter. Much of it is carried down to Lake St. Francis; however every year this ice forms a natural dam or jam in shallow localities and bends of the river that spring weather alone can break up. Years of experience has enabled us to observe that near Cornwall, at Crail island, at Weaver Point-a place located between Barnhard island and the Long Sault island-at Bradford, great ice-fields form. When the Long Sault dam is completed it is but logical to conclude that the ice, not being able to find an outlet in Lake St. Francis, will accoumulate up the river, from the autumn to the spring, hence the overflooding of canals, inundations and unavoidable havoc will be the result.
In the course of the years 1840, 1879, 1887, 1895, 1898 and 1905-serious jams occurred inundating part of the county of Dundas, carrying away buildings, etc.-We were thus enabled to form an idea of the consequences of such jams:	in a few hours the town of
Longueuil was flooded owing to the rise of the waters above the systems of drainage of towns neighbouring the ice-fields. Montreal was forced to build up special ramparts to protect itself and was obliged to install pumps in its draining system to protect itself against the rising water. With his ice-breakers, the Minister of Marine renders great services in the lower St. Lawrence. The artificial causeways at Long Sault will unavoidably and regularly raise the waters, create floods and their natural consequences because, even after the dam has been constructed, the swiftness of the current will still exist, carrying the frazil formed on a stretch of 10 miles of open water which accumulates from the autumn; above this artificial obstacle, anchor ice will form and the spring will accumulate there its ice-fields from less agitated waters, with results that are easily conceived.
This formation of frazil has the effect of greatly interfering with water-powers by impeding the flow of water, which obliges companies like the Cedar Rapids to have recourse to dynamite and gangs of men to remedy this nuisance.
Does my hon. friend believe that by completely damming the Long Sault-with the accumulation of ice over a stretch of many miles-a water-power will be able to develop its electric energy efficiently and produce it at a lower rate than those of other localities where these natural obstacles would not be encountered, and these powers we would be at liberty to acquire?
Besides the inconveniences which I have just enumerated the construction of a dam at the

upper end of Long Sault island and at the foot of Barnhard island the narrowest parts of the river, would mean the closing up of navigation through the Cornwall canal, an entirely Canadian enterprise; it would mean a diversion of 50 per cent of Canadian waters through the South canal, on American soil, when we own 76 per cent of these international waters; that would reduce the efficiency of the canals in regard to safeness of navigation and diminish the interest tourists have in this locality.
With the knowledge that nature creates an irresistable force when water and pack-ice come in conflict, may we not rightly believe,, that at a given moment, in a river of the size of the St. Lawrence, this dam may give way and cause disasters along the flooded area-from Cornwall to Montreal-as it has happened in other countries and even in our own country. In the present instance, what would be the damages sustained in the town of Cornwall, at the Soulanges canal, and even in Montreal? The scheme must assuredly need a great deal of consideration.
If this enterprise carries with it serious physical objections which make it difficult and dangerous to put into practice, and to say the least uncertain, there are other obstacles no less important as to their consequences. I mean in regard to the international viewpoint. Here are the facts: " This international stretch of country, commonly known as the Long Sault rapids is actually governed by the treaty of Ashburton which states that the north and south canals should be free of all obstacles and should only be used for navigation." This treaty would first have to be abrogated. A dam would be built at the upper end of Long Sault island so as to divert 50 per cent of Canadian waters into the United States territory, 86 per cent of the water-power would be within United States territory, the outlay for the erection and development of the waterpower and the dredging of a canal 25 feet deep, from Montreal to the head of the great lakes, would be equally shared by the United States and Canada. The United States would acquire freedom of access and trade on the St. Lawrence. There would be joint management of the enterprise. This is in a few words the plans of our neighbours. Judging by his resolution, the hon. member for Toronto Northwest is opposed to Canadian private interests regulating the level of the St. Lawrence waters; yet, what is most extraordinary, he would allow foreigners to perform this work! It is rather amusing to see him depart from the motto of his party and his own: "No trucking with the Yankees!" and then to meet him on the shores of the St.

St. Lawrence Waterway-Mr. Deslauriers
Lawrence crying out at the top of his voice for co-operation with these same Yankees, in connection with this scheme which, after all, would transfer from Canada to the United States 500,000 horse-power, under joint management, as the output of the St. Lawrence is
200,000	cubic feet per second with a drop of 30 and some odd feet.
If the hon. member for Toronto Northwest will take the trouble to examine our international relations with our neighbours, in the light of history, before taking such a step, he will be one of the first to admit the danger arising from such an enterprise. It is entirely wrong for a good citizen who has the interest of his country at heart, who is loyal to the British crown, to subscribe to such a scheme. Yesterday only, in the matter of the diversion of the waters of lake Michigan, the rights of Canada were ignored by the hon. member's friends of to-day. We have not forgotten the annexation terms of the Alaska peninsula, the States of Washington, Minnesota, Vermont and Maine, once Canadian territory, and, we are also fully aware how they look upon our rights in the Newfoundland fisheries.
Do we not know as a matter of fact that the debentures of the cities of Montreal and Toronto-not to mention almost all the debentures of our municipalities and provinces -are in the hands of New York financiers? We are aware that our lumber and pulp industries belong to them-SO per cent of the capital invested in those industries is American-and the same thing exists in our textile, rubber, glass and automobile industries. When we know the part played by United States capital invested in our water powers and mines, when we witness every day Americanism creeping into our literature, theatres, music and commerce, when financially the Canada of to-day seems to belong to them, one can naturally question whether the hon. member is still logical with himself in upholding his title of British citizen. If the love of his country, Canada, and that of his mother country do no more strike a sympathetic note in his heart, if in the presence of the American dollar his loyalty to the Empire has become but vain words and he wishes so eagerly to surrender to the United States the St. Lawrence, the armature of the richest colony of the British Empire, one may question whether he has shares in the seventy-one cruisers of the United States navy.
I protest against such schemes which aim at favouring the interests of our neighbours to the detriment of ours and places the weaker
at the mercy of the stronger-pursuant to the solemn practice of ages-at a time when war taxes burden the Canadian citizen. A project comprising the dredging of the St. Lawrence to a depth of 27 feet and the development of a water power of 1,000,000, horse power would cost, according to the American estimate and those advocating the St. Lawrence waterway, a sum of $252,428,000 and $2,562,000 per year for its administration, yet we know that these figures are put forth simply to lead one astray, because that amount does not include the interest on the invested capital in the course of carrying out the work, neither does it include the outlay for the dredging of ports on the lakes, nor the further outlay for dredging the rivers which connect the lakes-for it is an accepted fact that ocean liners are not built for the lakes no more than lake vessels are built for the ocean. It is acknowledged that even if ocean liners could sail up the lakes, they could not compete with lake vessels, even if we made allowance for the trans-shipment of their cargoes at Montreal.
Why should we be drawn into such a scheme, when we have at our door a project far more advantageous from every viewpoint -entirely within Canadian territory-a shorter route, less costly and capable of developing 3.500,000 of Canadian horse-power against
1,000,000 horse-power under joint management, and which would permit us to be the masters in our home.
The United States possess 16 per cent of potential energy at the Long Sault rapids; if they are short of electricity, let them utilize that power by damming the south canal at the foot of the Long Sault island, and let them follow the same procedure as in the Cedar rapids development; they will then have all that belongs to them and not 50 per cent of our electric energy as the present scheme calls for. That is all we can concede to them on behalf of the " bonne entente."
Any person who has the least knowledge, who knows American mentality and its ways of doing business must understand the purport of Senator Malby's bill introduced in the United States senate; it amounts to taking possession of our water powers without consulting us.
We must bear in mind the statements of Senator Chas. Townsend when he submitted to the Bureau of the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, on May 25, 1913, and again on March 17, 1914, a bill which was no other than the project of the hon. member for Toronto Northwest.
This senator expressed himself very clearly when he stated that this measure had no
