St. Lawrence Waterway-Mr. Deslauriers
other aim than to prevent the construction of the Georgian Bay canal, a scheme entirely Canadian and approved by all the prime ministers of Canada; the purport of the measure was to allow the United States to make use of our water powers on the St. Lawrence, control the transportation of Canadian grain and give them a navigable route into the very heart of their country by connecting with the Mississippi river. We cannot blame them for endeavouring to promote the interests of their country to the detriment of ours. But what are we to think of a Canadian who sides with them against his own country? We may strive to emulate them to a certain degree, but we would appear very childish if we thought that our neighbours were going to spend hundreds of millions to develop millions of horse-power for us, and dredge water routes to promote our interests, when the whole year round they treat us to embargo and prohibitive legislation. Certainly not. Let us provide for the future as well as they do, for are we not aware that their coal resources have been wasted, worked without discrimination and to such an extent that, to-day, we can foresee the date of their complete exhaustion; do we not know that in 30 years the iron mines of the Ohio valley, like the coal mines of the Appalachian deposits will be exhausted? Therefore, if we have been far-sighted citizens, we shall be in a position to see the same advantages as those of the city of Pittsburg and the Ohio valley transferred to the Ottawa valley where iron deposits are abundant and unexplored. The development of these mines by water powers, instead of coal would be more economical and capable of competing loyally with any country in the world, we shall witness all this on condition that we remain masters in our own country.

speakeroldname: Mr. H. C. HOCKEN (Toront West Centre):
speechtext:
I am wholeheartedly in support of the principle of the resolution which my hon. friend (Mr. Church) has introduced to-day. For a number of years I have been convinced that the construction of this waterway would do more to promote the prosperity of Canada than any other single enterprise that has ever been undertaken or that is in prospect at any time in the future; and it is with some degree of satisfaction, sir, that I go back to the session of 1924 in order, if you will permit me, to give to the house a few of the sentences I spoke on this question at that time. I was dealing then chiefly with what I considered to the best means of assisting the western farmers, the grain growers and those who come from the prairie provinces, and I said on that occasion that the farmers of the

west would have more to gain from the cheapening of transportation than from the removal of any tariff. I continued:
I would exhaust the resources of this country in cheapening transportation from western Canada to the seaboard.
That is the statement I made at that time. I went on:
The great thing is the development of the St. Lawrence river so that ocean vessels will go up to the head of the lakes, as they did last year, and take cargoes of wheat right over to Liverpool. I do not think that is the inevitable or the natural development of that route; but if the St. Lawrence river were improved to give a twenty-five or thirty foot draft, big ships that take 500,000 bushels of grain would load at Fort William and Would probably break bulk at the city of Quebec. . . A vessel holding 500.000 bushels of wheat would leave Fort William, go down to the city of Quebec and discharge into ocean boats which would go across to Liverpool, or to any other port in the world, in that way saving five to eight cents a bushel on wheat. If from five to eight cents a bushel could be saved on the wheat that was grown on the western prairies last year, the leader of the Progressive party can figure out what that meang. That is one of the ways in -which transportation can be cheapened. Water transportation, as we all know, can be done at much lower rates than rail transportation.
I venture to quote that statement made by myself in 1924, because not only have I seen no reason to change my views, but rather the course of my study of the question has led me to see greater advantages than I was able to discover then. In my opinion, the whole of Canada, from the Alberta boundary to the Atlantic ocean, would derive an enormous benefit from the construction of this waterway. I doubt very much that a large quantity of grain will ever go out by the Hudson Bay route. I voted for that undertaking, but not with any great enthusiasm. I believe the inevitable outlet for the produce of the west is to the head of the lakes by rail, and from the head of the lakes to Quebec by boats loading half a million bushels of grain, thence to be carried throughout the world to any port to which it might be consigned.
It is estimated that there will be a saving to the grain growers of Saskatchewan and Manitoba of ten cents a bushel on wheat. Let us suppose that it will be eight cents a bushel. One has only to consider the volume of wheat and other grain grown in that part of the country to realize what an enormous saving that will be. And remember that every dollar of that saving would go into the pockets of the farmers, the original producers. I believe that Ontario will benefit probably less than the west, certainly less than other provinces, because the province of Quebec will have then the two greatest ports in North
[DOT] .

St. Lawrence Waterway-Mr. Hocken
America. Not only will the grain of the northwest, and probably the cattle as well, go through Montreal to Quebec, but similar produce of twenty different states in the United States will be shipped by that route. We have to consider the organization that has taken place in the middle western states to promote this enterprise in order to realize how much dependence they place upon it as a relief from the high cost of transportation.
It has always been a matter of surprise to me that the western provinces of Canada should be so indifferent to this project while the middle western states of the republic should be so keenly alive to its advantages. I do not know how to explain that difference; I leave it to my hon. friends to my left. It may be that they have been so obsessed with the value of the Hudson bay route; that would explain it in part. But although this is a plan, the consummation of which is certain to save about eight cents a bushel on the transportation of their wheat, there has been remarkably little enthusiasm for it in the west. It would certainly result in an interchange of commerce among the different provinces which would do more than any other single thing to bring about that much desired national unity about which we are talking all the time. One has but to consider the volume of traffic that would pass over that portion of the St. Lawrence running through the province of Quebec to realize what it would mean to that province; and one can catch a glimpse of the prosperity that would result in the maritime provinces from the completion of this enterprise. It would make it possible to bring cargoes of
10.000	tons of coal right up to lake Erie. I do not suppose that Nova Scotia coal will ever do much on lake Erie, which is so close to the American mines. But Nova Scotia coal should go to Hamilton, where there is a great coking plant, to Toronto and to other cities along the lake Ontario coast. The maritime provinces would gain in another way. My opinion, which of course I venture with some hesitation-because I have reached the age when I have ceased to be dogmatic about anything-
Hear, hear.

You will get there too.
My opinion, I say, is that these great bulk cargoes of wheat would go to Halifax; and either at Quebec or at Halifax there should be developed the greatest milling centre in North America. Flour leaving Canada should go from Halifax or Quebec, but to-day Buffalo is the great milling centre, because it is at the end of the water transportation route
from the head of the lakes. We should make the end of that route somewhere on the St. Lawrence river or at Halifax, where flour could be shipped instead of wheat. If that development should take place, which I think is very probable, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick would become great cattle raising provinces; the by-products of the flour would provide feed for the cattle. These two provinces are well watered and suitable in every way for the raising of cattle, with the exception of feed, and with that one defect remedied they should become exceedingly prosperous in that particular industry. So it is not only the western provinces which will benefit through a lower cost of getting their produce to the markets of the world1; it is not only Ontario, which would probably receive a great quantity of its package freight direct from the ocean, or the province of Quebec, through which all this traffic would pass and whose cities would grow enormously in consequence; the maritime provinces also would receive great advantages. We sometimes do not think of them as particular beneficiaries under this project, but they would prosper just as much as any other province in this whole Dominion.
I am not going into details just now, Mr. Speaker, because that perhaps will be done later, and I would not like to embarrass the government by laying down a policy for them to follow.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
You are doing very
well.

I do not care whether this measure is introduced by the government or by the opposition; I am for it all the way through. The more I have thought about it during the last four years the more firmly I have become convinced that it is the greatest and most advantageous scheme which can be undertaken by the people of this country. It does not require much thought to realize that producers in the United States are going to enjoy equal advantages; they have to pay higher railway rates than are paid by hon. gentlemen from the west. They stand to gain perhaps more in proportion than the farmers on our Canadian prairies; therefore they are more deeply interested in this question than are the Canadian people, although without us they could not possibly go on with the enterprise. I absolutely support my hon. friend in what he has said, and I do so with enthusiasm; I trust that when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) brings down the correspondence having to do with this matter it will show that the government is deeply in earnest in its desire to carry on this great
1938	COMMONS
St. Lawrence Waterway-Mr. Hocken
enterprise as soon as arrangements can be made with the American republic to join with us in it.
Perhaps I differ from some of my friends on this side of the house in believing that this should be a joint enterprise, but as I have travelled from the head of the lakes down through the St. Marys, St. Clair and Detroit rivers and the Welland canal, it has been brought to my attention very clearly that already the United States has spent enormous sums of money in improving transportation channels even in Canadian territory. This country is now committed as fully as it can be committed to the joint enterprise; we have this joint work on the rivers from lake Ontario up to Fort William. The Welland canal is used by our friends from across the border on the same terms as it is used by our own people, and most if not all the channels between lake Erie and Fort William have been constructed partly at least by the expenditure of money on the part of the adjoining republic. So we have already undertaken this joint enterprise, and having regard to the amicable relations which exist and which I trust always will prevail between the two countries; having regard to the treaty under which they use our canals on the same terms that we use them, it seems to me there can be no argument against undertaking this great work in collaboration and co-operation with our friends to the south.
I just wanted to say these few words, Mr. Speaker, to put myself on record as being behind this enterprise just as strongly as possible. If I have any influence at all it will be exerted in support of the scheme, regardless of the source from which it may emanate, because I believe it is going to be a great thing for Canada and will do more to develop this country than anything else I can call to mind at the moment.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman who has just resumed his seat (Mr. Hocken) states that he is strongly in favour of this project. I am also in favour of completing these waterways some time in the future, but I do not believe Canada is in a financial position at present to accept the heavy obligations which would be entailed. Altogether aside from that, a great deal is being promised which seems rather absurd. I have a paper here in which a writer makes the claim that on our western grain we will save 12 cents a bushel, while the last speaker stated that the saving would be from 5 to 8 cents a bushel. A year or so ago I looked up the cost of carrying grain by rail from the transfer points of Owen Sound

and Collingwood to Montreal, and found it at that time to be 5.80 cents per bushel.
Where was that from?

From Owen Sound and Collingwood to Montreal. About 1908 or 1909 the entire cost of carrying grain from Fort William to Montreal was 4 cents a bushel; I think the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) will remember that, because he and I looked over the same book.
Yes, and I have the speech of the hon. member right here.
That was the all-water route?
I could not say; I think part was by rail, but it may have been all water.
It would not be part rail at the 4 cent rate.

The rate was 4 cents, anyway. Before this resolution came up I had intended to look up the rate for last year, but was unable to do so. I have heard it stated, however, that last year the rates were about 6 cents, and I have another statement here to the effect that a year ago the rate was 9 cents. This matter has no reference to the Welland canal; it deals only with the deepening of the St. Lawrence, so how are you going to save from 5 to 8 cents a bushel on wheat over a distance of only 135 miles when the whole rate from Fort William to Montreal varies from 4 to 12 cents? The whole proposition is absurd.
Can the hon. gentleman explain the reason for the difference between the 4 cent and the 12 cent rates?
During the war the cost of everything went up; prices doubled and trebled, and that was the reason for the high rate.

What was
the rate last year?

I am not sure. I heard
it stated it was six.

Now let me take up another point. I am very glad indeed that we have such friendly relations with the United States; it is something to be proud of, and it is a lesson to the rest of the world. Yet at this time, while some may think it would not be wise to review any instances of friction between the United States and other

St. Lawrence Waterway-Mr. Millar
countries in past years, I think that in dealing with this matter it may be well for us to consider what difficulties other countries have had with the United States in connection with proposals similar to this.
In the year 1850 the United States and Great Britain agreed on what they call the Clayton-Bulwer treaty to build the Panama canal on the basis of equal construction and equal control. The United States seem to have fretted under this treaty, and some time later they persuaded Great Britain to agree to another treaty, called the Hay-Paunce-fote treaty of 1901. In this Hay-Pauncefote treaty of 1901 it was provided that.
The canal shall be free and open to the vessels of commerce and war of all nations observing these rules on terms of entire equality, so that there shall be no discrimination against any such nation or its citizens or subjects in respect of the conditions or charges of traffic or otherwise.
However, in the face of this, after this treaty had been agreed to the United States congress at once turned around and passed the Panama Canal Act, which provided that no tolls should be levied upon vessels engaged in the coastwise trade of the United States. Great Britain took the view that this was a violation of the former treaty, and there was a great deal of friction about it. The Hearst papers of the United States madie much ado about it; organizations sent resolutions to congress and to the president, and a great deal was said about tlhe impudence of Great Britain in objecting to this act. However, later on, after a considerable amount of discussion. President Wilson abrogated this act and did what was fair and right to Great Britain.
Let us look for a moment at the experience of Colombia in connection with the Panama canal. If Great Britain's experience was an unhappy one, so certainly was that of Colombia, formerly New Granada. The new canal ran through Colombian territory. By a treaty entered into in 1846 the United States guaranteed positively and efficaciously to New Granada the perfect neutrality of the before-mentioned isthmus (Panama) with a view that the free transit from the one to the other sea might not be interrupted or embarrassed at any future time while the treaty existed; and in consequence the United States also guaranteed in the same manner the rights of sovereignty and property which New Granada had and possessed over the said territory.
In the year 1903 a treaty known as the Ilay-Herran treaty, negotiated between representatives of the United States and Colombia
and providing for the construction of the canal, was ratified by the American senate but rejected by Colombia. The constituent state of Panama, a portion of Colombia, traversed by the new oanal, thereupon declared its independence; a rebellion took place. In connection with this rebellion the independence of Panama was declared on November 3rd, 1963, and the United States recognized the independence of this state on November 6th, three days later. President Roosevelt who was in office at the time of the occurrence, afterwards declared:
I am interested in the Panama canal because I started it. If I had followed the precedent in such cases I should have submitted a dignified state paper to the congress and the debate would be going on yet. But, I took the canal zone and let congress debate.
An American commentator, Carl Russel Fish, remarks:
Its real excuse was rather the plea by which Jefferson justified himself in the Louisiana purchase,-the plea that the situation was one which could never happen again and was of such unparalleled importance as to exempt it from the ordinary laws of morality and of nations.
A matter that I think the government should very carefully study before this project is undertaken is the effect upon the levels of the upper lakes. It is a trite remark of recent years that the levels of the upper lakes as well as of the lower lakes have fallen considerably.

Will the hon. gentleman let
me interrupt and ask: Is the house to infer that if a treaty between the United States and Canada became effective, and the project was consummated, we would be in the same position as in connection with Panama?

I just leave the house to
draw its own conclusions. This is what took place in connection with Panama. I might go a little further in that connection. Not only did the United States recognize the independence of that state three days after they declared their independence, but on the 18th of the same month they made a treaty with them. A sequel to it was the memorial of Panama to the United States in June, 1923, requesting that government to declare that it "now holds all land necessary for the protection of the waterway, thereby affording a safeguard against expropriation which might eventually result in the absorption of the entire republic,"-a memorial yet unheeded. Colombia had had part of their land taken away, and when they tried to prevent the secession of Panama by armed force, they were prevented by the United States from doing so. The United States, as I have
1940	COMMONS
St. Lawrence Waterway-Mr. Millar
pointed out, recognized the independence of Panama three days after they had declared it, and on the 18th of the same month made another treaty with the newly recognized state.
I believe the last speaker stated that boats would likely load grain at Fort William and carry it to Quebec. That is indeed very doubtful. There are 44 miles of canal on the St. Lawrence, and a great many locks, and the insurance rates are high. It is doubtful whether large boats would take their loads of grain down through those canals with the probability of coming 'back empty; the cost would be too great. At present grain is transferred to smaller boats carrying 70.000,
75,000	and some of them as much as 90,000 bushels. The comment we would make, as grain growers of western Canada, is that the difference between the present rate and that which we might secure would be nearer one or two cents a bushel than six, eight, nine or twelve cents.
It must be remembered that this route would be open for only six or, at the most, seven moths of the year. Moreover, when a canal competes with a railroad the railroad usually takes the greater share of the trade. Competition between open water and rail gives a great advantage to the open water channel. The cost of the open water route, I believe, is about one-eighth-some have put it at one-tenth-the cost of an all-rail route; but that does not hold good for a canal where boats can travel at only about four knots an hour, which is the average, and where there is danger of their being held up, having to wait for their turn, or being crowded against the side, with possible consequent damage. It is very doubtful whether this route alone could compete with the rail route.
I am glad that some who are studying this matter are beginning to be doubtful about the wisdom of the government's proceeding at once. In my hand is a clipping containing a report of a meeting held at Kitchener. It states:
A number of the speakers were strongly opposed to any loophole which would give American interests the slightest chance of gaining a grasp upon the solely Canadian section of the waterway. There was a very considerable feeling that those parts of the ship canal which lie entirely within Canada should be owned and controlled exclusively by Canada.
We have over-built our transportation facilities; we have made a mistake in going so far in the building of trunk lines, and our railways are finding difficulty in earning dividends. It cannot be denied that if a new route is opened up, if it is going to accomplish what is claimed for it, if it is going to carry more of Canadian

and United States grain to Montreal, some of that traffic will be taken from the railways, which will find it even more difficult than they do now to make profits. [DOT]
I regret that so much of the argument consists in promises of what this new route is going to accomplish for western farmers. I realize that it is really a power project. As such it may succeed, although I do not know so much about that. It seems on the surface that there may be difficulty in developing water power that we do not need at present in Canada. If this surplus power is sold it must be sold to the United States, and after establishments are started there and are using this power, it will be most difficult to get it back. But apart from the water power I think it should be recognized that as grain growers, we are not particularly in need of this development and we do not see very much advantage in it. It may result in a lower rate on grain but the reduction will be very slight. Some time ago, when the joint commission was appointed, Mr. Hoover, in the course of a speech on this question in Canada -I believe it was about the first speech he had made in this country-to my surprise, and I think to the surprise of many, stated that the joint commission would bring in a report favourable to the project. That was an astonishing statement to make, but it was so reported in the press at the time.
I do not care to add anything further to what I have said in regard to this project. I am not against it, but I believe the government would be well advised to study very carefully these matters in relation to the United States and particularly the effect on the level of the upper lakes. In fact it might be found after a thorough investigation that it is not possible to deepen this channel without seriously affecting those levels. If that should ever be found to be the case, I do not think it would be wise to proceed with the plan. A loss of one foot of water in regard to carrying power means a great deal, and that loss falls upon those who are paying for the carrying of the goods. A loss of one foot of water on the upper lakes would cost millions of dollars to the farmers of western Canada through higher rates on their grain.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to detain the house at any considerable length, because I believe there are a number of other members who wish to say a few words in regard to this project. I rise because I believe somebody from my section of the country should once again put himself on record on this question.

St. Lawrence Waterway-Mr. Manion
I am on record on it so often, I must confess, that a statement of my views to-day does not really matter very much. May I say before I go any further that I am of course speaking entirely for myself, as other members who -have spoken to-day were speaking entirely for themselves?
I have had the fortune of following my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle (Mr. Millar) once or twice before on this question. I happened out of curiosity to look up Hansard of 1923, and I found that at that time he spoke on the question much along the line he took to-day, and I spoke much along the line I intend to take now; so that at least two members of this house have been entirely consistent on the question. I made a few remarks also in 1921 in favour of this project. As the papers are going to be tabled so soon, perhaps it would have been as well-and I rather hoped it would have turned out that way-had the whole debate been adjourned following the speech of the hon. member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church), because we cannot really intelligently discuss the question until those papers are produced. Whatever remarks I make, however, will be very general.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle spoke of a rate as low as four cents from the head of the lakes at a certain period. There are low rates at certain seasons; there are other seasons when the rates are very high, and of course those are the seasons when the heavy grain traffic is taking place.
The four cent rate was for a whole season.

I think my hon. friend said that that rate was in force about 1908. Of course, freight rates as well as everything else have gone up since 1908; but Julius Barnes, who is perhaps one of the best authorities, if not the best in the world, on grain, made the statement that the building of this canal would mean a difference of ten cents per bushel on wheat shipped to the old land. I believe he meant by that that the saving would be ten cents a bushel in taking the grain from Chicago, Duluth or Fort William to the old country. I think he included everything, and did not merely take in the lake and rail route.
Did he not mean taking the grain from the whole central United States on the average?

I have read his speech a number of times and his statement was very clear that this would mean a saving of ten cents a bushel. I have not read his speech for some years, but I believe he said in one
part of it that the building of this canal could be carried on every year by the saving that would be effected by the farmers of the United States in the transportation of grain. That is a pretty strong argument. Mr. Herbert Hoover has also taken pretty much the same attitude. It is a well known fact that the transportation of freight by water over a long haul is only about one-sixth or even one-tenth the cost of rail transportation.
Would my hon. friend make a comparison between the railway cost and the canal cost?

I have not the figures at
hand, but I presume that the canals would run the cost up. I do not claim to be an expert in any way, and I am speaking probably entirely as a theorist, but it has been stated many times by experts that you can carry a cargo from New York to Calcutta and a cargo from New York to Bombay at exactly the same cost, although there is a difference of 2,000 miles in the distance. That is because of the cheapness of water transportation.
When this question of the St. Lawrence waterway comes up there are some who attempt to make fun of the advocates of this route-I noticed an attempt in one newspaper to-day-suggesting that they expect the Olympic or the Mauritania to come right up to Toronto and perhaps to Fort William. But those who look at this question intelligently never expect any such thing. Those who regard the route as a feasible one do, however, believe that the grain of the west could be shipped from Fort William and Port Arthur bve water right through to Montreal, there to be transhipped on to the ocean-going boats. It is not believed by anybody of intelligence that there will be any regular system of ocean-going boats coming up the lakes, although I remember thirty years ago seeing a Norwegian boat at the head of the lakes, and foreign boats have been coming there ever since, although not on a large scale.
It should be remembered that the building of the Panama canal has made a complete change in the routing of traffic between the east and the west of the United States, and even between the eastern and the western part of Canada. One prominent manufacturer told me not long ago that he could ship his goods from a point near Toronto to Vancouver via the Panama canal more cheaply than he could ship them by rail across the continent. That illustrates very markedly the importance of water transportation. The building of the Panama canal has certainly been a very great blessing to the port of Vancouver. I venture to say that the port of Vancouver for the last
1942	COMMONS
St. Lawrence Waterway-Mr. Manion
few years has been the most prosperous city of its size in the Dominion, and that is largely because of the building of the Panama canal.
Then, of course, there also comes in the question of power development. It is estimated that between four and five million of horse-power can be developed on the St. Lawrence between Kingston and Montreal. There also enters into the question the fact that it will reduce the transportation costs on wheat, and a difference of only a few cents a bushel means a great deal to the farmers of the west. The development of this route would also mean that coal could be brought from Nova Scotia to the central portion of Canada. The development of this route is ultimately bound to come. Whether now is the time to make a start is a debatable question, and there are men just as sincere as I am who believe that we are premature in even discussing the matter at all at this time, while others think we are lagging behind in not making a start now. But ultimately this route will be developed in spite of all opposition from any section of the United States or of Canada, and when it is developed it will mean a much greater consumption of Nova Scotia coal in the central portions of Canada. And that is only as it should be, because it does seem to me a shame, when we have in this country the second largest coal deposits in the world, that we should be importing so much coal from the United States-$60,000,000 worth last year. The development of this route would mean the consumption of Nova Scotia coal to a very large extent in the central portions of Canada, and that would be a great blessing to Nova Scotia.
After spending $120,000,000 or thereabouts on the Welland canal-for that will be about the amount when it is completed-it seems to me that the building of this other waterway is the logical thing to do to round out the whole scheme. It will enable us to go down the lakes right to Montreal, which is 500 miles closer to Liverpool than is New York, and that is a factor of some importance. It is also to be remembered that about one-third the area of the United States, one-third of the population, and perhaps one-third of the production of that country, is tributary to this canal system through the great, lakes. Taking all these things into account I do not see how anyone can definitely take the stand of absolutely opposing this scheme, though of course anyone has the right to do that just as much as I have the right to support it.
I shall not take up further time, Mr. Speaker, because I understand there are others who wish to speak on this question, but in [Mr. Manion. 1
a general way I wish to give what little support I can as an individual member of this house to the hon. member who introduced the resolution.

One cannot listen to those who address the house on this motion without realizing that the whole question is one that simply bristles wt'ih difficulties. It is not as though we had no information, because from the date of the report of the International Joint Commission. which I believe was in 1921, there have been others well qualified and well equipped who have investigated this question in all its aspects and have made a report, and there is still another advisory board which has yet to make its report to this house. It seems to me that the air would be cleared to an appreciable extent if we could have the report of that advisory committee tabled. Having that, and having copies of the correspondence which the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has undertaken to lay on the table at an early day, we shall have information which will enable us to discuss the various features which my friend from Qu'Appelle (Mr. Millar) has discussed with some knowledge and without groping so much in the dark as we are obliged to do at the present moment.
While I welcome the opportunity afforded by the resolution moved by my friend from Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church), I would not dream at the present moment of seeking to have this house compel the government forthwith to enter into a treaty in regard to the matter. We have not the information which has been asked for, and which I believe is being prepared and will be before us in a very short time.
My friend from Qu'Appelle has brought into the discussion queries as to cost, as to the relations with the United States of America, as to the levels of the upper lakes, and probably other questions of which I took no note, but all queries which have been for a long, long time before the various bodies which have been authorized to consider the matter.
Let us assume for a moment that we do find from the final reports that come to this house, and from the discussion on the reports which this house will have an opportunity of engaging in, that the scheme is feasible from an economic standpoint, that there is no danger of international complications, that the levels of the upper lakes and of the lower lakes and of the St. Lawrence will not be interfered with. Of course, we must be satisfied on these points before we can enter into

St. Lawrence Waterway-Mr. Geary
such a tremendous undertaking. But assuming all that, and these difficulties being out of the way, would any hon. member of this house say that it would not be a wonderful thing for Canada that there should be a spearhead of navigation, so to speak, thrust into the very middle of the country? I will not speak of any benefit the United States may derive from that. If they benefit we need not be envious or jealous of them so long as it is a good thing for our own country. When we realize t'he vast resources in minerals stretching from central Manitoba at least, eastward to the province of Quebec, where geologists tell us we have an extension of the pre-cambrian shield bearing tremendous mineral deposits; when we realize the potentialities of that country in the development of minerals, potentialities which would come much closer to realization if we had this sort of transportation at the very doors of the mines; when we picture the industrial activity that would follow with waterborne traffic passing the doors of central Canada to the eastern and western provinces, it seems to me nobody can dispute the fact that the country would be tremendously benefited by such a state of affairs. We must rely on those general principles after disposing of the questions of cost, internationl complications, and so on, that have been raised. I suggest to the government that at as early a day as convenient and practicable all the information collated by the advisory committee be placed before this house for consideration. Then we shall have the last word on the subject, and many of the questions bothering members at the moment will be disposed of.
We have heard it said that Canada's main difficulty is a geographical one, that we have such a stretch of country from west to east as to make it almost impossible for adequate communications to be established. Well, as I look on this project in the large, to my mind it presents an opportunity of remedying one of the disabilities to which Providence has subjected us. I have often been surprised to hear my friends sitting in this house, particularly those representing western constituencies, state that the idea of a St. Lawrence waterway has not taken hold of their imagination. 1 learned this afternoon from an hon. gentleman who sits to my left-in whom I have much confidence- that in the west there is a general feeling of disappointment at the results following the construction of the Welland canal, and a conviction that the great railway bridge along the north shore has not done the work which it was built to do. It was built as a grain carrier in the expectation that it would enable grain to be carried
to the seaboard at a comparatively low cost. In that regard the people of the west have been disappointed. When the third Welland canal was deepened great hopes were entertained in the west of a lowering of freight rates on grain, but it appears that very little reduction in the transportation costs ensued. It is a fact though that the Welland canal on that occasion was deepened only to such an extent as would enable it to be utilized in connection with the other canals along the St. Lawrence; that is to say, it was not deepened sufficiently to allow of the passage of deep draught vessels. The new Welland canal, which will be completed in a few years, will allow ships carrying half a million bushels of grain to pass into lake Ontario. At present ships of that capacity have to break bulk at Port Colborne, where their cargoes are transshipped to smaller vessels. The transportation cost by water from Port Colborne to Montreal has been at the rate of six cents a bushel for a little over one-third the distance for which grain is carried on the upper lakes at three cents a bushel. This higher cost is accounted for, I understand, by the greater overhead expense of handling smaller ships, and in various other ways which I am not in a position to discuss. It is said that if a 500.000 bushel cargo could be shipped by water from Fort William or Port Arthur to Montreal, there would be only a very small increase in the three cent rate to Port Colborne. Of that I know nothing more than one can gather from different quarters, but when we get the report of the advisory committee perhaps we shall be able to deal with that as a matter of fact rather than as mere conjecture.
But looking at this project in the broad sense, as I say, it occurs to me that from the eastern edge of this country to the western, granted that the economic difficulties are removed, there can be nothing but benefit as a whole from the deepening of the St. Lawrence waterway. It is quite possible, as my hon. friend "from Toronto West Centre (Mr. Hocken) said, that grain could be carried down to Halifax and handled at large milling establishments to be erected there, and the products shipped across the ocean all the year around, and that coal from the maritime provinces could be shipped to the central provinces and even further west. Such a proposition would undoubtedly be very attractive to the people down there. My friends from Quebec are not particularly enamoured of this project, and I can only hope that such facts and arguments as may be placed before them will convince them that they are in error in opposing, as they do to some ex-
1944	COMMONS
St. Lawrence Waterway-Mr. Geary
tent, the construction of the St. Lawrence waterway. Take Ontario; if one or two of our sister provinces object, I am quite prepared to admit that we cannot proceed with an undertaking of this magnitude, for it must be considered as an undertaking for the benefit of Canada as a whole, not for one section or the other. We cannot expect the Dominion to spend money for the benefit of Ontario alone. For my part I cannot see how the city of Toronto is going to be advantaged by having grain carried past its door, but it is very likely that it will derive benefit from the waterway And I am safe in saying that a great body of opinion in the province of Ontario is strongly in favour of the project.
This brings me to the subject of hydroelectric power, in which we in Toronto are very vitally concerned. We are running out of power. We have had to enter into a contract with a power company in Quebec to tide us over the shortage. That power has to be transmitted three hundred miles from the Gatineau to the city of Toronto and the surrounding district. It is not a contract with which we in Ontario are very well pleased, for we think we are paying a pretty heavy rate for the power. When we get power from the St. Lawrence our difficulties will be solved for a long time. It has been estimated that all power generated in the St. Lawrence to be allocated to Canada will soon be absorbed in thie Dominion, and Ontario's share amounts from one to one and a half million horse power. Quebec, it is estimated, will have available some 3,000,000 horse power for distribution and use within the province, with all the consequences arising from cheap, adequate and easily transmitted. electrical energy. The province of Quebec I imagine, must look forward to a tremendous industrial development from that source alone.
Now I come to the west. I do not think that my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle means to say that because the grain growers see no particular benefit from the St. Lawrence waterway they are going to oppose the project. I think better of them than to believe that. I do not think, simply because such an undertaking might not in his view be of any particular personal value to him or the grain growers whom he represents, that he will object to it on that score. The Hudson bay route will do a certain amount of business; then there will be competition from the port of Vancouver; and if competition is increased by waterborne traffic from the head of the lakes at least as far as Montreal, surely 
in the end that must enure to the benefit of the western farmer and lighten his burden of transportation charges. My friends from British Columbia need not be afraid that they will be harmed by this enterprise, because after all competition is the life of trade, and competition in grain carrying cannot help but have some effect upon freight and waterborne traffic rates via Vancouver.
At the moment, Mr. Speaker, I have complete confidence that this enterprise will be of advantage to the whole Dominion, and that it should be proceeded with at the earliest possible date. All I can urge upon the government is that without delay they place the house in possession of all the facts in order that we may have an opportunity of studying them, and also in order that they may be broadcast throughout the whole Dominion so that every one may be in a position to decide for himself that this enterprise, whether from the standpoint of dollars and cents, of international complications, or from any other point of view, is not going to hurt Canada but rather is destined to be of inestimable benefit to the country at large. We have a very clear pronouncement by the chairman of the Montreal harbour board, who sees nothing but good for the city of Montreal in the St. Lawrence waterway. That statement is disputed in some quarters, as is every other statement that is made. I do not think that we should get into that state of mind in which we should want to be fighting between province and province and city and city. We must consider this not as a party question, not as a political matter; one party should not seek to get any particular advantage from it as against another. We should regard the matter as one upon which the future of this country depends in a marked degree. The matter looms up as so important that this house could not devote itself to anything with greater hope of reward than it could to the sympathetic consideration of the construction of this immense waterway.
At the moment we are stopped at Port Colborne. All that immense lake-borne traffic stops there, and we know that transhipment takes place at Buffalo. For economic reasons there is a considerable development there- a tremendous milling centre, where a great deal of Canadian grain is milled, some of it mixed with grain of an inferior quality. As soon as the Welland canal is opened we shall be able to go as far as Prescott. Are we going to stop there? Is that narrow gap between the St. Lawrence, the greatest waterway in the world, and the upper lakes, Ontario included, to be bridged, or are we going to stop at the stage we have reached? The

St. Lawrence Waterway-Mr. Mackenzie King
matter, I repeat, is one of vast importance; it may have an effect on the future of Canada such as we cannot comprehend. This house should consider the question from a Canadian standpoint, as effectively and thoroughly as possible, each member contributing his best to the consideration of it in the hope that we may arrive at the solution of a problem which, as I have said before, and as I say again, even at the risk of undue repetition, seems to be the most important before the people of Canada at this moment.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Most hon. members who have participated in the debate have, I think, very wisely recognized that, in the absence of important reports and documents bearing upon this great question, it would be inadvisable for anyone to attempt to give a final expression of his own views. I am sure the house will agree that in suggesting on behalf of the government that no effort be made to press the present resolution to a conclusion, but rather that the debate be adjourned until at least all the documents are before us, I am taking a course which is very much in the interests of all parties and certainly in the interests of the country.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
On Tuesday, on the resumption of the sittings of the house, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) inquired when the despatches on the St. Lawrence waterway project would be tabled, and I stated that I had communicated with the Secretary of State at Washington, expressing the hope that they might be tabled very shortly after the Easter recess. My communication had been sent to Washington prior to the recess. I may now say that it has been agreed between the two governments that the papers shall be given to the press on Monday night of next week. They will be tabled in this house at the time of adjournment, so that in both countries, so far as the press is concerned, the information will be available for the morning papers of Tuesday. Monday night the correspondence will be given out in both countries.
I agree with what my hon. friend (Mr. Geary) has said, that it would be advisable to include, in whatever documents may be brought down at that time, the report of the advisory committee, who have made a lengthy and careful investigation of the matter. The essential features of this report were brought to the attention of the United States government in connection with the communications which have passed between the two countries.
As a matter of convenience to all members of the house, and certainly as a convenience in all subsequent discussion of the subject, it might be well to include in the papers that are to be tabled on Monday night all of the important dispatches relating to the St. Lawrence waterway project, the dispatches that passed prior to the meeting of the advisory committee, the committee's report, and the dispatches that have passed since then up to the present time. It will be also of advantage, I believe, to place before the house the questions that are to be submitted to the courts touching the jurisdiction respectively of the Dominion and of the provincial governments in relation to power which may be developed as a consequence of the construction of works for purposes of navigation.
As hon. members know, the question of jurisdiction in the matter has been raised by the provinces and at the last Dominion-provincial conference a request was made of the Dominion government to refer to the courts, for a final decision, this important constitutional phase of the subject. The government at the time acquiesced in the request made, and I may inform the house that, as they will be presented to the courts, the questions will be agreed to by representatives of the provincial and of the Dominion governments. I understand that the Supreme Court will hear the reference on May 28, and probably an appeal may be taken to the Privy Council thereafter.
Have they been amended since the first draft was given to the newspapers?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I understand that, at the request of the provinces, one or two additional questions have been incorporated in the reference; but the questions except in this particular remain as they were originally drafted in the order in council. The provinces themselves-at least so I am informed-have suggested one or two further questions which will be added. It would, I think, be well to include among the papers to be laid on the table the orders in council governing the reference. By this means the house will then have before it all of the essential recent documents bearing on the St. Lawrence waterway project as a practical project and as one which has come to be the subject* of preliminary negotiations between the United States and Canada.

\\ ill the Prime Minister submit also the report of the engineering board, which was laid on the table but which has never been printed? I have asked several
1946	COMMONS
St. Lawrence Waterway-Mr. Mackenzie King
times at t'he distribution office for a copy of the report and I understand that so far it has not been printed for distribution.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: To what report does my hon. friend refer?

In the early days of the session the Prime Minister laid on the table the last report of the joint board of engineers. The report was not then in printed form and a motion was made to haw it printed and distributed. I have applied time and time again but I have not been able to obtain a copy of it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I regret the
fact; there must be some oversight. The report was printed and distributed and it is unfortunate that my hon. friend has not received his copy. I shall inquire.
I am glad to know that it has been printed, but I was told that it had not been.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Possibly I am in error in stating that the report was generally distributed. My impression is that it included some rather expensive plates, and it may be that only a limited number were struck off.

I shall be glad if the Prime Minister will see that I receive a copy, whether it includes the plates or not. A number of members on this side of the house have been applying continually to the distribution office, and these volumes have not been available. This is really one of the most important documents for our consideration.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The facts are, I think, that there are two volumes, one of the report and one of the plates. How extensive they are I do not recall at the moment; I know, however, they were quite large and it may be that they were not distributed to all the members on that account. In regard to a matter of this magnitude, however, I think the house should have before it, one might say almost regardless of cost, all the information which is essential, and certainly the government will endeavour to meet the wishes of the members of the house in that particular.
Now may I say that when the communications which have passed between the government of the United States and our own government are tabled, hon. members will find, despite what has appeared in the press and what has been hinted at by some of those who have spoken in debate, that so far no commitments have been made of a character which in any way will prove prejudicial to the

Dominion, to any province of the Dominion, to the influence of any hon. member of the house or any organ of public opinion in the country. From the outset the government have taken the view which has been expressed by many hon. members on both sides of the house, that the St. Lawrence project is one of the largest undertakings with which this country has ever been faced or is likely ever to be faced, and we have felt that in the preliminary negotiations we should proceed with the utmost caution, not with undue haste nor on the other hand with undue delays, but rather to make progress in the light of the importance of the project and in a way which will enable public opinion gradually to formulate and express itself. I believe it would be prejudicial to the ultimate success of any project of this character were steps to be taken prematurely which would give rise to doubt or to fear in the minds of the people of any section of Canada as to the w'isdom of the course which was taken. If the project, as I believe it to be, is one which will come in the course of time, and which has very much even now to commend it if certain economic considerations can be satisfactorily met, then it will be made all the more certain of accomplishment by being advanced cautiously, step by step, but always in the right direction. That is what the government have thus far attempted to do and I think, Mr. Speaker, with these words the house will probably support me in moving the adjournment of the debate.
Just before the Prime Minister concludes, after these papers are tabled, if the house so wishes I suppose there will be an opportunity for further discussion?

speakeroldname: Mr. H. B. ADSHEAD (East Calgary) moved:
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the time is opportune that according to agreement, the government of Canada should discuss with the government of Great Britain, the desirability of Canada accepting article 36 of the statutes of the Permanent Court of Internationa] Justice providing for compulsory arbitration in international disputes.

International Disputes-Mr. Adshead
He said:	Mr. Speaker, at this late hour it
is impossible for me to cover all the points with which I had intended to deal in connection with this most important question. Suffice it to sa}' that if the members of the house will look at page 23 of the report of the Imperial conference they will find that the question of compulsory arbitration is touched on. I do not wish to go into the details of the arbitration treaty more than to say in general that the countries which may subscribe to the arbitration treaty agree that they will arbitrate all their international difficulties without resort to war, with certain modifications and exceptions.
At that conference an understanding was arrived at, something as follows:	A general
understanding was reached that none of the governments represented at the Imperial conference would take any action in the direction of the acceptance of the compulsory jurisdiction of the permanent court without bringing the matter up for further discussion. So you will see that however desirable it may be that Canada, England, Australia, or any of the component parts of the British Empire should sign the arbitration treaty, they cannot do so. Canada's hands are tied; the hands of England, Australia, and all the members of the British Empire are tied until they bring up the matter for further discussion, and it is with this object in view that I have brought forward this resolution to-day. If this should pass the house, or if it strikes the government favourably, we might say to the British government: We are going to bring up that matter for discussion in order that our hands may be untied, so that if we wish to sign the compulsory arbitration treaty we may do so.
At present 26 nations have signed that treaty, and according to the latest report of the Empire Parliamentary Association, two more states, Germany and Guatemala, have signed, so I presume 2S nations have now signed it. It may be that when the government notify Great Britain that they propose to bring up the matter for discussion, some other and better method may be brought forward, but at any rate I hold that Canada should be free to sign that treaty if she so wishes, in common with any other component part of the British Empire.
There are other reasons why we should consider this matter. The other day Lloyd George said that perhaps the most disastrous war in history would occur unless the nations of the world saw fit to resort to something else than force, and unless they worked out some method of arbitrating their difficulties 56103-124
by right and by reason rather than by force of arms. Lord Rothermere has said the same thing, so I think Canada has good reasons for signing that arbitration treaty, or at least for bringing it up for discussion.
Then there is another point to be considered. I am sorry to say that if my information is correct, at present in England there is a very erroneous opinion prevailing among a large number of people that the dominions, Canada among them, are instrumental in tieing the hands of England; in other words, that England cannot sign the arbitration treaty because the dominions will not allow her to do so. In the issue of the Manchester Guardian of December 2 last appears some interviews and some speeches from some English statesmen. I do not wish to bring English politics into this house, but to my mind it is important that Canada should be placed in a right light before the English people, that we may not be looked upon as a deterring factor in this matter One of the gentlemen is reported to havi said that if England agreed to arbitrate anc the dominions did not agree to do so, England would find herself at loggerheads with the dominions. Again, Ramsay MacDonald is reported to have said, "It is not fair to blame the dominions." He spoke about Canada as probably being willing to accept the optional clause; and the reply was made that we did not sign the protocol. Then further it was said:	Well, if Canada and the
dominions are not willing to sign this thing, we should sign it whether they are willing or not. That is the attitude taken. There is a false impression that the dominions, Canada having been mentioned as one of the dominions, is one of the factors preventing England signing the clause by which she will settle her differences by arbitration rather than by war. To set ourselves right in our own estimation and in the eyes of the people of England and of the world we ought to pass this resolution and notify Great Britain that we are going to consider the optional clause, and that at the earliest opportunity we will discuss this matter in order to untie her hands and our hands as well, so that the false impression will not any longer exist.

Call it six
o'clock.

I do not know whether
I would be right in asking the government to make a declaration on this point. The time is getting late, and I should like the government to say something upon this point.
